questions.question: What does it mean for two sets $A$ and $B$ to have the same cardinality?
options: The sets have exactly the same elements.
There exists a bijection $f\colon A\to B$.
One set is a subset of the other.
There exists any function $f\colon A\to B$.

questions.question: Suppose $|A| = |B|$ and $A$ is a finite set with five distinct elements. What can be concluded about $B$?
options: $B$ must contain the same elements as $A$.
$B$ must be a subset of $A$.
$B$ has five distinct elements.
$B$ must be infinite.

questions.question: What is the cardinality of the empty set, $|\varnothing|$?
options: undefined
$\infty$

questions.question: Although $\mathbb{N}\subsetneq\mathbb{Q}$, the two sets have the same cardinality. Which fact accounts for this?
options: An injection from $\mathbb{N}$ into $\mathbb{Q}$ is enough for equal size.
Every rational number is a natural number.
There exists a bijection between $\mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$.
Both sets are infinite, and all infinite sets match.

questions.question: Can an infinite set have the same cardinality as a proper subset of itself?
options: Yes; e.g. $\mathbb{N}$ and the even natural numbers
No; a proper subset is always strictly smaller
Yes, but only for uncountable sets such as $\mathbb{R}$
Yes; e.g. $\{1,2,3\}$ and its subset $\{1,2\}$

questions.question: If $|A|=|B|$, does $|B|=|A|$ also hold?
options: Yes; bijection inverses are bijections.
No; cardinality is not symmetric
Only for finite sets
Only when $A=B$

questions.question: What is the cardinality of $\{1,1,2\}$ as a set?
For sets $A$ and $B$, which condition means $\operatorname{card}(A)<\operatorname{card}(B)$?
options: An injection $A\to B$ exists, but no bijection does
An injection $A\to B$ exists that is not surjective
No bijection between $A$ and $B$ exists
$A\subsetneq B$, so $B$ has elements that $A$ lacks

questions.question: The map $f\colon\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, $f(n)=n$, is injective but not surjective. What does $f$ by itself show about $\mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbb{Z}$?
options: It cannot settle equality; another map may be a bijection
$\operatorname{card}(\mathbb{N})<\operatorname{card}(\mathbb{Z})$, since $f$ misses $-1$
$\operatorname{card}(\mathbb{N})=\operatorname{card}(\mathbb{Z})$, since $f$ is injective
$\mathbb{Z}$ is uncountable, since $f$ misses infinitely many integers

questions.question: Do $\mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbb{R}$ have the same cardinality?
options: No; $\mathbb{R}$ is strictly larger than $\mathbb{N}$
Yes; both are infinite, so they match
Yes; $\mathbb{R}$ is countable, like $\mathbb{Q}$
No; $\mathbb{N}$ is strictly larger than $\mathbb{R}$
